name: Gauss's Law
statement: The electric flux through a closed surface depends only on the charge inside.
meaning: Take any closed surface of any shape and count the net electric field lines passing out through it. That net flux depends solely on how much charge is enclosed, not on the surface's shape or where the charge sits inside. No enclosed charge means zero net flux.
mechanism: The net flux equals the enclosed charge divided by the permittivity of free space. It is mathematically equivalent to Coulomb's inverse-square law: the field of a point charge falls as one over distance squared while a surface's area grows as distance squared, so their product — the flux — stays constant with size. It is one of Maxwell's four equations and, via the divergence theorem, links a surface flux to the charge within.

examples.text: Inside a hollow charged conductor no charge is enclosed by a surface drawn within it, so the field there is exactly zero — the reason a metal enclosure shields its interior from external fields.
For a sphere, an infinite line, or an infinite plane of charge, Gauss's law yields the field in a line or two, exploiting symmetry to pull the field out of the flux integral.
Since the field inside a conductor in equilibrium is zero, any surface drawn within it encloses no net charge, so all excess charge must sit on the outer surface.

variants.name: Coulomb's law
variants.text: The electrostatic law it is mathematically equivalent to, each derivable from the other given superposition or spherical symmetry — but Gauss's law extends to time-varying fields where Coulomb's does not.

variants.name: Gauss's law for magnetism
variants.text: The magnetic counterpart: the magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero, expressing the absence of magnetic monopoles.

whyItMatters: It is one of the four Maxwell equations and a cornerstone of electromagnetism, both a deep statement that charge is the source of the electric field and a powerful shortcut for computing fields of symmetric distributions. It generalises Coulomb's law to the full, time-varying theory.

working.text: for spherical, cylindrical, or planar charge distributions, draw a matching Gaussian surface and read the field off the enclosed charge.
conclude the field is zero, or unchanged, wherever a closed surface encloses no net charge, as inside a hollow conductor.

working.lead: Prefer it over Coulomb for the general case
working.text: reach for Gauss's law where the field is time-varying or the geometry is symmetric, since it is fundamental and general.

limits: Within classical electromagnetism the law is exact, not an approximation — it is one of Maxwell's equations and holds for static and time-varying fields alike, verified to extraordinary precision. Its only limitation is practical: it yields the field easily only when the charge distribution is highly symmetric, so that the field can be pulled outside the flux integral. Without such symmetry the law remains true but does not directly give the field, and one falls back on Coulomb's law, superposition, or numerical methods.
misreadings: The symmetry requirement is about ease of solving, not the law's validity — Gauss's law is always true, but it hands you the field only when the geometry is symmetric enough. And unlike Coulomb's electrostatics-only form, it is fully general, holding even for moving charges and changing fields.
origin: Formulated by Carl Friedrich Gauss in 1835, in the context of the attraction of ellipsoids, and published posthumously in 1867; Joseph-Louis Lagrange had reached an equivalent statement in 1773. It is now one of Maxwell's four equations of electromagnetism.

sources.text: Gauss's law, Wikipedia. — the statement, the Coulomb equivalence, the Lagrange/Gauss origin, and the symmetry-for-solving point.
"Gauss's law," Encyclopædia Britannica. — the flux-proportional-to-charge statement and Gauss's law for magnetism.
